learning_objective: 🎯 Understand runtime errors versus syntax errors, and master graceful program execution using Python's try-except-else-finally blocks and custom exception raising.

key_vocabulary.definition: An unwanted or unexpected runtime error that disrupts the normal flow of a program's execution.
An error caused by violating the grammatical rules of the programming language, detected before execution.
A Python statement used to explicitly throw an exception when a specific condition occurs.
A debugging statement that tests a condition and raises an AssertionError if the condition evaluates to False.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Syntax errors stop code from running at all because the code is grammatically invalid (e.g., missing a colon). Exceptions are errors that occur while a syntactically correct program is executing (e.g., dividing by zero or opening a missing file).

Risky code is placed in the 'try' block. If an exception occurs, control jumps to the matching 'except' block. The 'else' block runs only if no exception was raised in 'try', and 'finally' executes no matter what (used for cleanup like closing files).

Key built-in exceptions include ZeroDivisionError (dividing by zero), ValueError (wrong data value/type formatting), NameError (using an undefined variable), IOError/FileNotFoundError (file operations failing), and TypeError (unsupported operation between data types).

You can intentionally trigger an error using 'raise ExceptionName("message")'. Alternatively, 'assert condition, message' verifies sanity checks during development and throws an AssertionError if the condition fails.

exam_tips: 📌 Always order your 'except' blocks from the most specific exception child class (e.g., ValueError) down to the most general parent class (Exception), otherwise the generic block will intercept everything [1.1.1].
📌 Do not confuse 'else' and 'finally': 'else' only executes if NO exception occurred, whereas 'finally' ALWAYS executes regardless of errors.
📌 In code-output questions, watch out for integer conversion inside input (`int(input())`) — entering a string or float will trigger a ValueError, not a TypeError.
quick_recap: ⭐ An unhandled exception causes the Python interpreter to print a traceback and terminate program execution [1.1.1].
⭐ You can catch multiple exceptions in a single block using a tuple: `except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError):`.
⭐ The `assert` statement can be disabled globally when running Python in optimized mode (`-O` flag), so never use it for production data validation.
